summary: In-ear detection can make TWS earbuds feel more responsive by pausing media or changing power state when an earbud is removed. For private label buyers, the feature also creates questions about sensor placement, skin and hair variation, false triggers, enclosure space, power consumption, firmware logic and user instructions. This iSoud guide organizes those questions before sampling.

sections.title: Why wear detection is a product-system decision
body: Official hearables references from STMicroelectronics describe in-ear detection as one of the functions enabled by motion, proximity and other compact sensors. ams OSRAM also describes proximity sensing that can turn wireless earbuds off when they are not in the ear. These references show why wear detection is more than a line of packaging copy.

The final experience depends on the sensor, earbud geometry, optical window or sensing area, firmware thresholds, left-and-right logic, charging-case behavior and the variety of real users. A source-factory discussion should define the intended behavior first: auto pause, auto resume, low-power state, call handling or a combination of these.

sections.title: In-ear detection RFQ questions for private label earbuds
bullets: Does the model use optical proximity, motion sensing or another wear-detection method?
What should happen when one earbud is removed and the other remains in use?
Should media resume automatically when the earbud is reinserted?
How does the model behave during calls, voice prompts and single-ear use?
Can wear detection be disabled through touch controls or an app setting?
How are false triggers tested across different skin tones, hair, ear shapes and lighting conditions?
What is the expected power impact of the selected sensing and polling configuration?

sections.title: Sensor placement affects enclosure, color and finish
body: Small proximity modules can give designers more freedom, but the sensor still needs a reliable optical or sensing path. Dark finishes, glossy coatings, translucent windows, printed graphics and the curvature of the earbud shell can affect the industrial-design conversation.

For custom color projects, the buyer should approve the sensing area together with the final color and surface finish. A cosmetic sample that hides or changes the sensor window may not behave like the engineering sample. This is why CMF approval and functional validation should not be separated.
bullets: Mark the sensing area on the industrial-design drawing.
Test the final color, coating and optical-window material.
Check sensor behavior after logo printing and cosmetic assembly.
Review enclosure space together with battery, microphone and antenna placement.
Keep a signed functional sample as the mass-production reference.

sections.title: Auto-pause validation and packaging claim control
body: A useful validation plan covers insertion and removal speed, one-ear use, two-ear use, media pause, media resume, calls, charging-case storage, low battery and repeated daily movement. Buyers should record the approved firmware version and avoid claiming instant, universal or error-free detection without model-level evidence.
